neighbours.q: Why don't antibiotics work against viruses like the flu?
neighbours.label: medfacts
neighbours.reply:
Antibiotics are designed to target and kill bacteria. They work by interfering with the processes that bacteria need to survive and reproduce, such as attacking their cell walls or disrupting their ability to synthesize essential components.

Viruses, on the other hand, are much smaller and have a different structure and way of operating. They don't have cell walls like bacteria, and they don't reproduce by dividing like bacteria. Instead, viruses hijack the machinery of a host cell to make copies of themselves.

Because viruses don't have the same structures or processes as bacteria, antibiotics can't target them effectively. Trying to use an antibiotic against a virus is like trying to use a key designed to open a lock on a door when you need a different kind of tool to open a window.

In some cases, antibiotics can harm the body by killing off beneficial bacteria that live in our bodies, which can lead to serious health problems.
